judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 942. It bars discrimination in schools and colleges and treats anti-Semitism as a form of it. The act bans discrimination in public schools and state colleges. It covers students and workers alike. The grounds listed are race, ethnicity, national origin, sex, disability, religion and marital status. Classes, guidance, counseling and financial help must be open to all students on the same terms. Teaching aimed at students learning English, gifted students or students with disabilities is not affected. Nor is any Indian education program. Schools and colleges must also put a set definition of anti-Semitism into their codes of conduct. It is the one agreed by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance. They must treat anti-Semitic harassment as they treat harassment based on race. The state school department and the college regents must each name a coordinator. The coordinator takes complaints, looks into them, and gives a school thirty days to put things right. If a school does not, the coordinator reports it to the federal government. The act says it does not limit free speech. The Oklahoma House passed it 56-29. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 991. It adopts a set definition of anti-Semitism for the state to work from. The state adopts a working definition of anti-Semitism. It is the one agreed by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance in 2016, with the examples set out in it. The definition is not binding law on its own. It may be used only as a guide. The uses named are training, education, spotting hate crimes and bias, and tracking reports of anti-Semitic incidents. The act says it does not limit any right protected by the First Amendment or by the state constitution. The Oklahoma House passed it 62-24. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 250. It changes how much of a tipped worker's pay can come from tips rather than cash wages. Tips can count toward the minimum wage. Under the old law they could cover no more than half of it. So a tipped worker was owed at least half the minimum wage in cash. The act drops that half-wage limit. Instead the employer must pay the cash wage set by federal rule. That rule sets $2.13 an hour. Meals and lodging count the same way tips do. The act also covers what happens if the state minimum wage rises above the federal one. In that case an employer may still count tips, meals or lodging toward it. The change took effect on November 1, 2025. The Oklahoma House passed it 74-19. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 2084. It caps what a state college may pay a professor to settle a state-law claim of being fired unlawfully. Claims under federal law are not capped. The cap is two years of the professor's pay on the day they were let go. It applies to colleges in the state system. It covers every way a claim can end. That means a deal the two sides agree, an arbitrator's award, or a court judgment. Back pay, damages and any other money awarded all count toward the cap. Some things sit outside it. Those are retirement money already earned, unpaid wages and unused leave. Staff who are not faculty are not covered. Nor is any written contract with such a worker. The cap starts on November 1, 2026. The Oklahoma House passed it 70-21. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 998. It lets electric companies charge customers for new plant sooner and with less review. The Corporation Commission sets electric rates in Oklahoma. It now has 180 days to rule on a plan for a new power plant that runs mainly on gas. The old limit was 240 days. Bids taken in an open contest count as proof that the company weighed other options. The company may also start charging customers for a gas plant while it is still being built. That is before the plant makes any power. If the company drops the project, it must pay the money back with interest. The act adds one more route to charge customers. A company may set aside most of the yearly cost of new equipment and bill it later. The share is ninety percent. That balance goes into rates and is collected over twenty years. The Commission still checks that the spending was sound before the balance enters rates. The Oklahoma House passed it 51-39. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 658. It stops the state child welfare agency from ruling out foster or adoptive parents over their beliefs about sexual orientation and gender identity. The act tells the Department of Human Services three things it may not do. Each turns on a parent's sincerely held religious or moral beliefs about sexual orientation and gender identity. It may not make a parent affirm a government policy that conflicts with those beliefs. It may not refuse approval because of those beliefs. That holds even where the parent means to raise a child in line with them. And it may not rule such a parent out for a particular child on those grounds. The department may still weigh the beliefs of the child and of the child's own family. Every placement must still serve the child's best interest. The Oklahoma House passed it 68-19. The Governor signed it.
